summary.heading: What is fission?
summary.html:
• Nuclear fission: a heavy nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei of similar size (fission fragments), plus two or three neutrons and a large release of energy.
  • Neutron-induced fission: a nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits (as in reactors). Uranium-235 splits most easily with slow (thermal) neutrons, about 0.025 eV.
  • Spontaneous fission: some very heavy nuclei split on their own (e.g. californium-252, used as a neutron source).
  • Example: $^{1}_{0}\text{n} + {}^{235}_{\;92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{141}_{\;56}\text{Ba} + {}^{92}_{36}\text{Kr} + 3\,{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$. Nucleon number and charge are conserved; the fragments vary from one fission to the next.

summary.heading: The energy released
summary.html:
• Uranium has about 7.6 MeV per nucleon; medium-sized fragments about 8.5 MeV. The fragments are more tightly bound and have less mass, and the difference is released.
  • From the curve: about $236 \times 0.9 \approx 200$ MeV per fission.
  • From masses: $\Delta m$ = (total mass before) − (total mass after), then $E = \Delta m \times 931.5$ MeV per u. Include the incoming neutron before and all the released neutrons after.
  • Be able to give the change in mass as well as the energy, in u or kg ($1\ \text{u} = 1.661 \times 10^{-27}$ kg), and work backwards from an energy or power to a mass with $\Delta m = \dfrac{E}{c^2}$. Less than 0.1% of the mass is converted.
  • Most of the energy is kinetic energy of the fragments, which fly apart by electric repulsion; the rest goes to neutrons, gamma rays and the later decay of the fragments. In a reactor it becomes thermal energy.
  • 1 kg of uranium-235 releases about $7 \times 10^{13}$ J, millions of times more than 1 kg of coal.

summary.heading: Chain reactions and critical mass
summary.html:
• Each fission releases two or three neutrons. If at least one causes another fission, the reaction sustains itself: a chain reaction.
  • Reactor: on average exactly one neutron per fission causes another, so the rate is steady. Bomb: more than one, so the rate grows exponentially.
  • Neutrons are lost by escaping through the surface or being absorbed without fission. Critical mass: the minimum mass for a self-sustaining chain reaction (a small lump has too much surface for its volume).
  • Natural uranium is 99.3% uranium-238 and 0.7% uranium-235; reactors use enriched fuel with 3–5% uranium-235.

summary.heading: Inside a nuclear power station
summary.html:
PartRole
Fuel rodshold the enriched uranium (uranium oxide pellets)
Moderatorslows fast neutrons (about 2 MeV) to thermal speeds by collisions with light nuclei (hydrogen in water, carbon in graphite), so they are more likely to cause fission
Control rodsabsorb neutrons (boron or cadmium): lower them to slow the reaction, drop them fully to shut it down
Coolantcarries thermal energy away from the core (pressurized water, CO₂ gas or liquid sodium)
Heat exchangerpasses thermal energy to a separate water circuit to make steam, so radioactive coolant never reaches the turbine
Shieldingsteel vessel and thick concrete absorb neutrons and gamma rays
  • Energy chain: nuclear → kinetic energy of fragments → thermal energy of coolant → kinetic energy of steam and turbine → electrical. Overall efficiency about 33%; most is lost as heat at the condenser.
  • The lighter the moderator nucleus, the more energy a neutron loses per collision (momentum and energy conservation, A.2).

summary.heading: Power station calculations
summary.html:
• Thermal power of the reactor = electrical output ÷ efficiency.
  • Fissions per second = thermal power ÷ energy per fission (in J).
  • Nuclei per day = fissions per second × 86 400; mass = number × nucleon number × $u$.
  • Example scale: a 1.0 GW (electrical) station at 33% uses about 3 kg of uranium-235 a day; a coal station of the same power burns thousands of tonnes.
  • Write the units at every step: $\frac{\text{J s}^{-1}}{\text{J}} = \text{s}^{-1}$.

summary.heading: Fission products and nuclear waste
summary.html:
• Fission fragments have too many neutrons for their size, so they are highly radioactive (mostly β⁻ and gamma). Some are short-lived and intensely active; others last decades (caesium-137, 30 years).
  • Uranium-238 absorbs neutrons and becomes plutonium-239 (alpha emitter, 24 000 years).
  • Managing spent fuel: cooling ponds for several years (absorb radiation, remove decay heat) → reprocessing in some countries (recover uranium and plutonium) → vitrification (sealed in glass and steel) → deep geological repository.
  • Low-level waste (clothing, tools) is compacted and stored in shallower sites.
  • Long-term issues: isolating waste from groundwater for thousands of years, longer than any institution has lasted, and keeping plutonium from weapons use.

summary.heading: Fission and climate change
summary.html:
For nuclear powerAgainst nuclear power
Very low carbon emissions (lifetime similar to wind)Long-lived radioactive waste
Steady output whatever the weatherRare but serious accidents
Tiny amounts of fuel; little landExpensive and slow to build and decommission
Fuel reserves last a long timeRisk of materials being used for weapons

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Saying energy is released because "bonds break": the products have a higher binding energy per nucleon, so less mass.
  • Saying the moderator absorbs neutrons: it slows them; control rods absorb them.
  • Thinking fast neutrons cause fission better: in uranium-235, slow neutrons are far more likely to.
  • Forgetting the neutrons when balancing equations or adding up masses.
  • Saying a reactor can explode like a bomb: the fuel isn't enriched enough; accidents involve overheating, fires and steam explosions.
  • Mixing up electrical and thermal power in efficiency calculations.

Interpretation: Hahn had the data but not the explanation. Why might an expert chemist struggle to accept that a nucleus had split?
Meitner and Frisch used the liquid-drop picture and $E = mc^2$ to check their idea. What makes an interpretation convincing?
Collaboration: Chicago Pile-1 needed physicists, engineers and machinists. What does each bring that the others can't?
Wartime projects were secret. How does secrecy change the way science normally works?
Ethics: Should the scientists who built the first bombs be judged by the knowledge of 1945 or of today?
Is there any physics that should not be researched? Who should make that decision?
Risk: Find deaths per unit of electricity for coal, gas, nuclear and wind. Why do the figures and public fear differ so much?
How did Chernobyl and Fukushima differ in cause and in consequences?

oracy.html:
Structured debate (two teams, the rest as judges, 15 minutes): opening statements, rebuttals, then a vote. Motion: "Nuclear fission power stations should be a major part of our country's plan to cut carbon dioxide emissions."

  • Our main argument is …
  • The other team claimed …, but …
  • The evidence that supports this is …

Listen for: physics on both sides: the fuel's very high energy density, no carbon dioxide from fission itself, a chain reaction kept steady by control rods; but long-lived radioactive fission products that must be stored safely.

Are scientists responsible for how their: Meitner refused to join the Manhattan Project. Compare her choice with Fermi's or Oppenheimer's.
Is a scientist who discovers fission more responsible than one who builds the bomb, or less?
How do we compare risks?: Ask students to rank a list of risks by gut feeling, then compare with real statistics. Which ones surprised them, and why?
Why do rare, dramatic events seem more dangerous than common, quiet ones?
Can we make decisions for 10 000 years a: How would you warn people in 10 000 years to keep away from a repository, if they don't speak any language we know?
Do we owe anything to people who won't exist for thousands of years?
Who gets the credit?: Why was Meitner left out of the 1944 Nobel Prize? List possible reasons: gender, exile, the prize rules, chemistry versus physics.
Big discoveries now have hundreds of authors. Is credit for individuals still a sensible idea?

videos.title: Nuclear Energy Explained: How does it work? 1/3
videos.use: A five-minute overview of fission and a power station. Use it as a starter, then ask students to name the parts it didn't explain (moderator, heat exchanger).

videos.title: A chain reaction (with mousetraps and ping pong balls)
videos.use: The classic mousetrap model of a chain reaction. Ask what in the model plays the part of the neutrons, and how a control rod could be added.

videos.title: 3 Reasons Why Nuclear Energy Is Terrible! 2/3
videos.use: For the climate-change debate: show it alongside part 3/3 ("3 Reasons Why Nuclear Energy Is Awesome!") and ask students to judge the arguments.

alsoLabs.note: Collisions between carts of different masses: a way into why light nuclei make the best moderators. The lab's main topic is A.2.
